DASHBOARD.INTRO: A little understanding. A more thoughtful practice.
DASHBOARD.BASICS_BODY: Pilates brings attention to breath, movement and control. On a mat or apparatus, the aim is not the biggest movement: it is a movement you can perform with purpose. These six principles are commonly taught in contemporary Pilates.
DASHBOARD.UNAVAILABLE: The featured exercise is unavailable right now.
DASHBOARD.SAFETY: General education, not an individual exercise prescription. Choose movements appropriate to your experience and health. Stop if an exercise causes pain, dizziness or unusual breathlessness; seek qualified advice when needed.

PRINCIPLES.TITLE: Principles, put into practice
PRINCIPLES.SUMMARY: Six ideas that give movement purpose, without making it rigid.
PRINCIPLES.TIP: Choose a range you can manage smoothly. A smaller, deliberate movement is more useful than forcing the final position.
PRINCIPLES.ONE: Concentration means noticing what you are doing. Before a repetition, notice your support points and your breath. Control means being able to begin, change and finish the movement deliberately, not simply moving as slowly as possible.
PRINCIPLES.TWO: Centering directs attention to support through the trunk. It does not mean holding the abdomen tight throughout a session. Precision is choosing the intended movement while allowing the rest of the body to contribute without unnecessary tension.
PRINCIPLES.THREE: Breath and flow connect one phase to the next. Keep breathing and make transitions unhurried. These six ideas are a commonly taught framework, not a test of perfection or a reason to push through discomfort.
PRINCIPLES.CUE: Offer one clear intention at a time: 'Return as deliberately as you reach.' Watch the response before adding another cue.

BREATHING.TITLE: Breath and movement
BREATHING.SUMMARY: Use breathing as a rhythm, not another task to get right.
BREATHING.TIP: Let the ribs expand comfortably as you inhale. Avoid holding your breath to finish a difficult repetition.
BREATHING.ONE: In a comfortable position, notice where breathing moves your ribs. Allow them to expand on an inhale and settle on an exhale. There is no need to take the deepest possible breath or press your shoulders down.
BREATHING.TWO: Try matching an easy movement to an unforced breath. Exhaling during effort is a useful starting cue, but breathing patterns vary by exercise and teaching approach. Continuous, comfortable breathing matters more than matching a count exactly.
BREATHING.THREE: If you keep holding your breath, reduce the range, resistance or number of repetitions. Pause before trying again. Lightheadedness is a reason to stop, not a sign that breathing practice is working.
BREATHING.CUE: Try 'Let the breath continue as you move.' Allow time for a natural breath instead of asking everyone to match your breathing speed.

ALIGNMENT.TITLE: Alignment without rigidity
ALIGNMENT.SUMMARY: Find useful support and build movement from there.
ALIGNMENT.TIP: Notice contact with the mat or apparatus. Let that support help you move without bracing your neck or jaw.
ALIGNMENT.ONE: Alignment is a relationship between body parts and the movement you are doing. There is no single pose to hold for every exercise. Begin with a comfortable, supported position and follow the setup for that specific movement.
ALIGNMENT.TWO: Explore only as far as you can maintain the intended action and breathe comfortably. Bending the knees or reducing a reach may make an exercise more manageable. A modification is a useful choice, not a failed repetition.
ALIGNMENT.THREE_TITLE: Progress one thing at a time
ALIGNMENT.THREE: When a movement feels consistent, change one demand: range, resistance, repetitions or coordination. More is not always better. If pain or a health condition affects your movement, seek individual guidance before progressing.
ALIGNMENT.CUE: Ask 'Where do you feel supported?' Observe breathing and movement quality before suggesting a larger range or extra resistance.

WATCH.TITLE: Your class, on your wrist
WATCH.BODY: Use an Apple Watch or Wear OS companion to see the current exercise, its countdown and what's next.
WATCH.CONTROLS: Go, pause, resume or stop from your watch. Stop asks for confirmation.
WATCH.WAIT: With auto-advance off, each new exercise waits for Go. Change this in Settings.
WATCH.PHONE: Your phone runs the class. Keep FlowSmith open in the foreground and your paired phone nearby; the watch is not standalone.
WATCH.WEB: Watch support requires the native FlowSmith phone app, not a browser. Setup differs by platform:
WATCH.IOS_PAIR: Pair your Apple Watch with your iPhone using Apple's Watch app.
WATCH.IOS_INSTALL: Install FlowSmith on your iPhone and its Apple Watch companion through the Watch app.
WATCH.ANDROID_PAIR: Pair your Wear OS watch with your Android phone using the watch manufacturer's companion app.
WATCH.ANDROID_INSTALL: Install FlowSmith on your Android phone and the matching FlowSmith Wear OS companion on your watch.
WATCH.LOAD: Then open FlowSmith on both devices and load a flow into Run on your phone. Your watch mirrors the class; use Go when ready.
WATCH.RECONNECT: Controls are unavailable when disconnected. Reopen FlowSmith on both devices and check their connection. No watch? Continue the tour and use your phone.
